item.title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
item.author: Rutian Huang, Xiao Geng, Xinyu Wu, Genting Dai, Liangliang Yang, Jianshe Liu, and Wei Chen
item.content:encoded:
This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustableinductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.

Rutian Huang, Xiao Geng, Xinyu Wu, Genting Dai, Liangliang Yang, Jianshe Liu, and Wei Chen

item.title: Cavity-assisted dynamic nuclear polarisation
item.author: Tristan Lorriaux, Yutian Wen, Patrice Bertet, Benjamin Huard, and Audrey Bienfait
item.content:encoded:
Dynamic nuclear polarisation transfers polarisation from electron to nuclear spins by relying on a dissipative channel. Here we introduce a cavity-based DNP mechanism which uses theradiative relaxation of the electronic spin through the Purcell effect to bring about the nuclear spin polarisation. We implement this protocol on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins (I=9/2, S=1/2) in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator. A single cycle, combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation, increases a target ground state’s population by a factor of 1.79±0.04; a cumulative enhancement of 4.6±0.2 is reached with additional cycles, to be compared with the theoretical limit of ninefold set by the degeneracy of the ground manifold. We explain this difference by the competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation on the one hand and a collective effect that slows down the electronic spin radiative decay as the nuclear spin population grows on the other hand. Our results place radiative DNP as an available mechanism at millikelvin temperatures where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen.

Tristan Lorriaux, Yutian Wen, Patrice Bertet, Benjamin Huard, and Audrey Bienfait

item.title: Modelling Josephson Junctions with Boundary Conditions: Towards High-Fidelity Models for Superconducting Qubits
item.author: Luis Bueno Blanco, and Juan Manuel Pérez-Pardo
item.content:encoded:
Josephson junctions are the central nonlinear element of superconducting qubits, yet their standard description is reached through a chain of approximations. We propose a purely quantum-mechanicalmodel of the junction, formulated directly in Hilbert space: a charged particle moves on a one-dimensional loop, and the junction is a point at which the wave function obeys self-adjoint boundary conditions, labelled by a coupling strength λ, which controls the transparency of the junction, and a phase jump δ, which plays the role of the superconducting phase difference. For a loop with a single junction we solve the spectral problem and show that the ground-state momentum expectation, identified with the supercurrent, factorises exactly as ⟨p̂ 0⟩=Ic(δ,λ)sinδ. For opaque junctions Ic becomes independent of δ and the first Josephson relation I=Icsinδ is recovered; for strongly attractive coupling, where the ground state is bound to the junction, the sinδ law is also recovered, but with an exponentially suppressed amplitude. For more transparent junctions, however, the model \emph{predicts} deviations from the pure sinδ law: Ic acquires a dependence on δ already at order λ−2, compatible with the higher Josephson harmonics recently found necessary to describe superconducting qubit spectra, and a fully transparent contact yields a current linear in δ. When the phase varies in time, a gauge transformation shows that the voltage drop across the junction is proportional to δ˙, so that the second Josephson relation emerges without being imposed. The boundary-condition approach thus reproduces both Josephson relations from first principles and predicts corrections to them, offering a route towards higher-fidelity models of superconducting qubits.

Luis Bueno Blanco, and Juan Manuel Pérez-Pardo

item.title: TLS loss in superconducting resonators on epitaxial hBN thin films
item.author: J. Christiansen-Salameh, D.J. Temples, R. Linehan, S. Sussman, Aloyse Maille, F. Abouzahr, L. Alexis, K. Anyang, D. Bowring, G. Bratrud, E. Celi, A.H. Colón Cesaní, R. Khatiwada, D. Molenaar, O. Peek, A. Rodriguez, O. Seidel, D. Schlom, D. Sotir, S. Uemura, Y. Wu, E. Figueroa-Feliciano, D. Baxter, and Z. Tian
item.content:encoded:
The integration of low-loss dielectrics into superconducting circuits is of importance to the functionality of quantum computers and sensors. In this work, we fabricate and measureniobium resonators atop few-layer, epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy on a sapphire substrate and compare against a control counterpart without hBN. We conduct radiofrequency measurements which probe the responses to power, temperature, and temporal fluctuations of two-level systems. The resonators integrating hBN maintain low dielectric loss with a low-power internal loss tangent on the order of 10−6, and demonstrate hBN can be added to the conventional superconducting qubit stack with minimal degradation of the quality factor. This research represents a first step towards a materials-driven strategy to eliminate phonon-mediated correlated errors in solid-state quantum systems, which leverages the thermal properties of 2D materials to prevent athermal phonons excited in the device substrate from transmitting across the superconductor-substrate interface. The same technique applied to quantum sensors would maximize phonon collection by blocking phonons from entering passive metal films.

J. Christiansen-Salameh, D.J. Temples, R. Linehan, S. Sussman, Aloyse Maille, F. Abouzahr, L. Alexis, K. Anyang, D. Bowring, G. Bratrud, E. Celi, A.H. Colón Cesaní, R. Khatiwada, D. Molenaar, O. Peek, A. Rodriguez, O. Seidel, D. Schlom, D. Sotir, S. Uemura, Y. Wu, E. Figueroa-Feliciano, D. Baxter, and Z. Tian

item.title: Quantitative Rules for Parallel Calibration and Drift-Resilient Maintenance of Large-Scale Superconducting Quantum Processors
item.author: Zhihao Wu, Kechengqi Zhu, Shichuan Xue, Xinfang Zhang, Zhaohua Yang, Zhida Zhang, Shun Hu, Cong Li, Dingdong Liu, Kangding Zhao, Peng Luo, Lingling Lao, Xiang Fu, Mingtang Deng, Junjie Wu, and Kai Lu
item.content:encoded:
As superconducting quantum processors scale toward hundreds of qubits, manual calibration becomes increasingly costly and difficult to sustain. Here we address two system-level factorsgoverning automated calibration, namely, crosstalk induced by parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters. On a 66-qubit superconducting processor, cross-entropy benchmarking shows that single-qubit calibration tolerates full-chip concurrency with minimal fidelity loss, whereas CZ calibration requires a minimum coupler-graph distance of four to avoid elevated control errors. Continuous monitoring of representative qubit and coupler parameters further yields quantitative refresh rules that assign refresh priority by error-budget consumption. These results turn two conventionally heuristic choices, the concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority of each control parameter, into measurable operating rules. Implemented within an automated calibration framework, the rules support a six-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with a zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity of 89.64%, distance-dependent logical-error suppression in a single-cycle repetition-code benchmark, and a reduction of the mean single-qubit error from 0.023 to 0.011 on a 337-qubit processor, providing an experimentally grounded reference for the automated calibration and maintenance of current and future large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

Zhihao Wu, Kechengqi Zhu, Shichuan Xue, Xinfang Zhang, Zhaohua Yang, Zhida Zhang, Shun Hu, Cong Li, Dingdong Liu, Kangding Zhao, Peng Luo, Lingling Lao, Xiang Fu, Mingtang Deng, Junjie Wu, and Kai Lu

item.title: A quasiparticle-protected superconducting qubit
item.author: Trond Hjerpekjøn Haug, Johan Kolvik, Joey Frey, Paul Burger, Fabian Resare, Witlef Wieczorek, Simone Gasparinetti, Per Delsing, and Raphaël Van Laer
item.content:encoded:
Superconducting quantum circuits underpin large-scale quantum processors and are increasingly interfaced with optical systems, yet they are vulnerable to quasiparticle poisoning fromhigh-energy radiation and optical fields. Gap engineering of Josephson junctions suppresses quasiparticle-induced relaxation, but quasiparticles near the junction can still shift the qubit frequency and cause phase errors. Here, we extend gap engineering beyond the junction using a flux-tunable transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and strongly gap-engineered aluminum junctions designed to keep quasiparticles away from the junction leads. Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, we demonstrate that the niobium device withstands more than an order of magnitude higher near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appears. The Nb transmon shows no resolvable quasiparticle-induced frequency shift over the same power range. At the same time, we observe that dephasing and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity increase with optical power even while relaxation remains protected. These results suggest that engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the junction can substantially increase qubit resilience, not only to radiation-induced error bursts, but also to nearby optical fields.

Trond Hjerpekjøn Haug, Johan Kolvik, Joey Frey, Paul Burger, Fabian Resare, Witlef Wieczorek, Simone Gasparinetti, Per Delsing, and Raphaël Van Laer

item.title: Quantum Simulation of a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System with Superconducting Circuits
item.author: Han-xin Che, Yangyang Yu, Tao Zhang, Wen Zheng, Hai-Feng Yu, Xinsheng Tan, and Yang Yu
item.content:encoded:
Hyperbolic geometry hosts a plethora of exotic quantum phenomena ranging from holographic duality to novel topological phases. However, investigating these effects experimentally remainschallenging due to the Euclidean constraints of natural crystalline materials. While recent synthetic lattices have achieved static realizations, they often lack the dynamical tunability required to explore the full geometric landscape. Here, we overcome these limitations by implementing a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit. We construct a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) by mapping the hyperbolic properties onto the dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters. By probing the systems‘ response under geometric quantum driving, we elucidate how the intrinsic geometry of the parameter space dictates observable physical quantities. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical framework to realize ensemble simulation. This generalization enables us to harness the fast coherent control of superconducting qubits to capture essential geometric characteristics, establishing a versatile platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds.

Han-xin Che, Yangyang Yu, Tao Zhang, Wen Zheng, Hai-Feng Yu, Xinsheng Tan, and Yang Yu

item.title: Sub-MHz SWAP spectroscopy of two-level systems in superconducting qubits
item.author: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, and Loren J. Swenson
item.content:encoded:
An outstanding challenge in superconducting quantum circuits is mitigating loss from two-level system (TLS) defects. SWAP spectroscopy with flux-tunable qubits can detect individualTLSs, but the Rabi chevrons that signal coherent exchange have been observed only for the most strongly coupled defects. Here, we introduce a sequence with fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout, switched off during the energy-relaxation delay for finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times. We detect Rabi chevrons at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, an order of magnitude lower than previously reported. In the dressed-state picture, we fit the coherent swap oscillations to extract the TLS energy-relaxation time. These Rabi chevrons reveal coherent TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, at coupling strengths previously associated with incoherent TLSs. The swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise, indicating that the dressed gap protects them from low-frequency 1/f noise.

Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, and Loren J. Swenson

item.title: Geodesic-based optimal control for leakage suppression in superconducting qubits
item.author: Adonai Hilário da Silva, Tanmoy Pandit, and Francesco Cosco
item.content:encoded:
Superconducting qubits are often based on the first two energy levels of a physical anharmonic LC oscillator. Since the anharmonicity of such systems is usually much lower than theinvolved energy gaps, population can easily leak to higher energy states. This is what characterizes leakage errors, and it can have multiple sources: from coherent error induced by the control platform to incoherent thermal dissipation. In this work, we adapt an optimal control method based on sub-Riemannian geodesic search in the unitary group for a system consisting of two superconducting qubits with leakage levels. We use the Rx(π/2) rotation for single-qubit operation analysis, and the iSWAP operation for two-qubit analysis. For the former, we find considerable performance improvement in average gate fidelity as well as in the reduction of leakage errors when comparing the obtained optimal pulses with Gaussian and DRAG pulses, especially for short duration pulses. For the iSWAP gate, although leakage error remains roughly the same, we manage to obtain considerably higher fidelities with the cost of requiring a slightly longer time evolution.

Adonai Hilário da Silva, Tanmoy Pandit, and Francesco Cosco

item.title: Stimulated emission for a three-level artificial atom in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
item.author: O. A. Chuikin, Ya. S. Greenberg, V. V. Taravkova, and O. V. Kibis
item.content:encoded:
This work is devoted to a theoretical study of the interaction of a quantum three-level ladder system with a continuous electromagnetic field in a one-dimensional open waveguide. Weconsider a situation closely resembling stimulated emission – the scattering of a single-photon exponential pulse by an excited three-level emitter. Using the real-space formalism, we obtain an analytical expression for the wavefunction of our system. We show that, for the low anharmonicity of a three-level system inherent to a transmon (the most common type of artificial atom), the influence of the third level can have a significant effect on the system’s behavior. Namely, the presence of the third level largely suppresses the stimulated emission effect if the relative anharmonicity is lower than |αr|<4%. However, for a three-level system, it is possible to obtain correlation effects such as photon bunching in the reflected field, which can also be 'switched off' by tuning the incident photon parameters.[/expand]

O. A. Chuikin, Ya. S. Greenberg, V. V. Taravkova, and O. V. Kibis
